De Rust

By: Diana Lucas | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

Summary:
Driving from Johannesburg to Cape Town, on the N12 National Road though the Karoo, it’s about 100 kms after Beaufort West that the arid landscape transforms from flat grey to yellow, stone boulders that increase in numbers until you are driving into your own yellow brick road fantasy, through sandstone cliffs and crystal-clear mountain streams that form the imposing Meiringspoort Pass, a 25 km gorge – part of the Swartberg Mountain range.

This is the entry to one of South Africa’s most charming dorps, the gateway between the Great Karoo and Little Karoo. The main road curves through the Victorian heritage buildings, broekie lace and a flock of sheep …. Combined with curiously named shops – the ‘pink elephant’ wine shop, Mengelmoeskardoes where you can delve into yester years. Rusty Nail, the bar… Karoo Rouge with its collection of veld skoene –


Further information:
Exploring the town we will find and come across the Museum,, the original Post office, the graveyard, quirky scenes and fascinating inhabitants like:

Hotel De Rust- the original hotel, first opened in 1953. It was the gathering place for the community. The owner Roy Shamely’s deep love affair was with art which he filled his hotel with – he also owned the filling station next door both were magnets for the community to gather. But when a piece of art was stolen from the hotel in 1990, Roy closed it downl and lived there alone until he passed away in September 2021. It’s now re-opened by his grandson.

Anne Meiring, is a descendent of the man who discovered the access through Meiringspoort, hence the name. She has stories to tell of her ancestor, Petrus Johannes Meiring who found work as fore man on the original farm, Petrus discovered the deep cleft through the Swarberg linking the little to the Great Karoo and was later instrumental in the first road through the pass in 1858

The there’s Pieter le Roux and Swepie le Roux, both descendents of the original settlers who established De Rust in the late 1800’s. They have tales of the Boer war, the rise and fall of the ostrich industry.

Jan and Theresa Venter own House Martin a lodge ion the Main Street, Schoeman Street, they are both involved in the community. Jan is on the Greater Oudtshoorn/De Rust Tourism Committee.

Take a walk through Meiringspoort pass to the waterfall with the Local Chief of the First Nation (getting his name) who will tell us the history of the Khoi/San in the De Rust area.

Jenny Bischoff a local artist, whose hand painted mural welcomes you to De Rust
Jenny draws creativity from the peaceful surroundings of De Rust. Her design features local elements. She also makes baby slippers crafted from the pure merino wool
Numbi Valley, an off grid bountiful permaculture farm where the owners live in a cob house

Back on the Oudemuragie road towards Oudtshoorn is De Rustica, an olive farm whose olive oil won the worlds best olive oil last year. They do olive oil tastings a fine art in how to tell the difference between virgin and extra virgin olive oil.

This karoo dorpie is not just a blip on the map, a stop over for travellers. It’s not one of our many towns or dorps in South Africa living out its’ last years. De Rust is a dorp with a history, a creative community determined to not only survive but thrive in the changing landscape of South Africa.

Script:


DE RUST


Meiringspoort – One of the most beautiful mountain passes in South Africa.
The road is carved through 250 million year old layers of sandstone – a gateway between the Great Karoo and the Little Karoo.

Legend has it that a mermaid lives here, halfway down the poort, at the bottom of a waterfall.
But as intriguing as that sounds, our destination is a small town at the foot of the pass.
Now we are heading to De Rust in the Karoo to check if it’s really one of the best small towns in the country…the people that live there certainly think so.

V/O
There’s something about karoo dorpies, on the surface nothing ever seems to be going on, De Rust is no different, the streets are empty, there’s no one in sight…..

Except for a lone figure sitting on a stoep in the Main Street

Frieda and Mac say Hello

Freda I stand up every day and think how lucky I am to live here/


Freda Schoeman married into one of the three De Rust’s first families, the Schoemans…the Le Roux’s and the Meirings. She has lived here for 40 years.

Freda Up Sound: Dis hoekom dis Meirings port is, hierde straat is Schoeman Straat volgende is Le Roux Straat

It was Petrus Johannes Meiring who discovered a deep cleft in the Swartberg in 1820. In 1858 this became the first road through the gorge…Meiringspoort, and De Rust, was officially born.

Freda The family has been here since 1860. The farm where we live was built in 1860.
Mac How did they end up here and what were they doing?
Freda: It was a resting place. The towns were far apart and the transport was much slower. So they needed an outspan place. And that’s how De Rus started. It was the farm De Rust that was eventually converted into a dorp.


Today an estimated 500 people live in De Rust proper.

It’s one of the few Karoo towns that is growing with an engaged creative community determined to improve their town

Across the road from the Bouginvillea clad HouseMartin, where we are staying, is a monument to another decade – Hotel De Rust.


Werner: Hello Mac a very warm welcome to Hotel De Rust.
Mac: Thank you.


Werner Alberts is the owner

It was Werner’s wife’s grandfather Nick Shamely who built Hotel De Rust in 1954.

Mac When you walk in here feels like you are going back in time,
Werner Absolutely and that’s what our slogan is a step back in time.
Mac: A step back in time… and all this art where does it come from?

Werner: He loved art so he supported local artists. If you look at the picture you can see this is the Swartberg…there is the Komanassie Mountain so most of it is from surrounding area as they say Karoo and Country.


Nicks collection expanded into original movie posters and memorabilia he would hunt down….

Mac: So this is quiet an iconic sound?
Werner: It was used on trains so every the announcer would call you for breakfast he would walk through the … SOUND DING DONG


Maryna: It’s a small town we have stories
Mac: Love it SKINERY
Maryna: Of course….

V/O
Photographers Maryna Cotton and her husband Sarel Van Staden discovered De Rust during lockdown…
Maryna: We worked a lot in the Karoo we did a lot at SKA the square kilometre arrray….ended up doing some work for Nat Geo and that work was spotted by Coenie de Villiers and Deon Mayer

Ons Karoo was the result.

Maryna: That book brought us to De Rust and that’s how we ended up here. We came and never left

Mac This picture fascinates me it looks like a haunted house right but it’s also at night right? The texture is unbelievable I can almost see the green of the algae that’s growing on the building.
Maryna: So the textures are due to the technique. We love photographing the old ruins there many of them here. Beautiful old buildings and then you might have a little bit of roof left or walls. I wish I knew the stories.


Mac: Oom Swepie you didn’t have to come down the stairs
Swepie: Good Afternoon.

Someone who knows all the stories is 89 year old Swepie Le Roux, a third generation De Ruster.

Swepie: This is how we plucked the ostriches


A legend in these parts Swepie still farms on the original Le Roux farm, Doornkraal

Swepie: And there’s my Oupa and Dad working with the plumes.
.

V/O
Under Swepie, Doornkraall now not only has ostriches but harvests a variety of fruits, splendidly laid out for us.

Swepie: Oupa had only farmed ostriches he said to me you mustn’t farm just one thing, have a mixture you might not have lot of money but you will always have something

The culture of farming has changed, from Swepie’s Oupa’s time

Swepie: A bakkie boer you can’t be… later in his life he said what has become of us we sit in bakkies and order people around *



V/O
On the other side of De Rust is a more recent olive farm, Rustica -- which boasts a number of award-winning olive oils, like this Corotina...

Megan So you take a glass in your fingers like this OK
Mac: This is a Corotina, the award winning….
Megan This is the award winning olive oil..
Mac: Award winning olive oil….not castor oil, come right man
Megan: Ok you do the swirl, just to make sure you bring out all the flavours, all the aromas and all the characteristics.

VO
Olive sommelier, Megan Stuurman takes us through the tasting of 2023’s best,

Megan So it’s like a freshly cut green grass. The grass in the olive oil is always a reminder of how good this olive oil is going to be ok
So after you smell your olive oil ,then you take a small slip it’s actually very soft a buttery olive oil


Grumpy Goat
Up Sound mac coming in talking

.
V/O
It was on an evening like this at the Grumpy Goat that , Maryna came up with her BIG idea


Maryna: In all honesty I thought there was a little bit of wine involved
Mac: Aaah Brandewyn

V/O
…..A calendar of the towns - mostly middle aged man- in all their glory to raise money for a De Rust charity drive.

Maryna :It didn’t have the reception, they told me in no uncertain terms it wasn’t going to happen.
Mac: You are mad
Maryna: Amongst other things, and that was the polite stuff.. A couple of days later a few of them cornered me in town and said so when are we doing the calendar.

Mac: My favourite is December righ and only reason it’s my favourite because it sayst ‘Egte Afrikaans Boerewors’
Maryna Afrikaanse Boere spices I photographed them in their own business’s and that had to find props so you have bits and pieces of quirky personalities. Oom Swepie was also in the calender His only request was can I please keep my socks on…

Mac So Oom Swerpie I also heard you were a model, a model for a a calendar?

Swerpie: h everyone must have a scandal and you must take ownership of your decision. But I can tell you they had great powers of persuasion. They said you must be naked . I said. I am old with flappy, saggy skin, there’s not a muscle in sight. They said that’s alright you can hold a basket in front of you. That sounded like great fun and a lot of men were up for it but they were muscular guys. I said that’s alright there must be an old one too. You can see you scoundrels you are also going to get old.
Mac The towns father can also do it


V/O
Before we leave there’s one thing left to investigate..the mermaid at the bottom of Meiringpoort’s pool

Freda: I think for us living here it's just a legend but if it’s interesting for others let them search.

Link
I am here now and the story sort of makes sense I thought I would jump in greet the mermaid and see if she really exists I am going no where near that water have you seen how dark it is..nee
Dankie, leave the mermaid where she is bye bye water girl we will not see you, Fact
